'''''Mammillaria prolifera''''', commonly known as the '''Texas nipple-cactus''', '''West Indian nipple-cactus''', '''grape cactus''', or '''hair-covered cactus''', is a species of [[cactus]] native to North America. Three [[subspecies]] are currently recognized: ''M. prolifera'' subsp. '''''prolifera''''' (Cuba, Dominican Republic, and Haiti), ''M. prolifera'' subsp. '''''arachnoidea''''' (Mexico), and ''M. prolifera'' subsp. '''''texana''''' (Mexico and the United States). The subspecies differ in overall size, the number and color of the [[thorns, spines, and prickles|spines]], and the shape and color of the flowers. The plant's round or slightly elongated stems usually form small, dense clusters, and flowers are commonly born alongside fruit. It is one of the most popular and widely grown ''[[Mammillaria]]'' species.

==Taxonomy==
''Mammillaria prolifera'' was first [[species description|described]] in 1768 by [[Philip Miller]] in ''[[The Gardeners Dictionary]]''. Miller named it ''Cactus proliferus'', "commonly called Small Childing Melon-Thistle".<ref name="JohnPilbeam"/> Several modern common names are in use, including Texas or West Indian nipple-cactus,<ref name="iucn">{{cite iucn |author=Goettsch, B.K. |author2=Gómez-Hinostrosa, C. |author3=Terry, M. |year=2017 |amends=2013 |title=''Mammillaria prolifera'' |volume=2017 |article-number=e.T152479A121536725 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2017-3.RLTS.T152479A121536725.en |access-date=17 January 2025}}</ref> hair-covered cactus, and grape cactus.<ref name="Weniger"/> It is the second species in the ''[[Mammillaria]]'' [[genus]] to be described, after the [[type species]], ''[[Mammillaria mammillaris|M. mammillaris]]''.<ref name="JohnPilbeam"/> ''M. prolifera'' belongs to the Mammillaria [[clade]] of the genus. The most closely related species is ''[[Mammillaria senilis|M. senilis]]''.<ref name="Breslin">{{cite journal | last1=Breslin | first1=Peter B. | last2=Wojciechowski | first2=Martin F. | last3=Majure | first3=Lucas C. | title=Molecular phylogeny of the Mammilloid clade (Cactaceae) resolves the monophyly of ''Mammillaria'' | journal=[[Taxon (journal)|Taxon]] | publisher=[[Wiley (publisher)|Wiley]] | volume=70 | issue=2 | date=12 February 2021 | issn=0040-0262 | doi=10.1002/tax.12451 | pages=308–323| jstor=27124309 }}</ref>

Three [[subspecies]] are presently recognized: ''M. prolifera'' subsp. ''prolifera'', ''M. prolifera'' subsp. ''arachnoidea'', and ''M. prolifera'' subsp. ''texana'' ([[synonym (taxonomy)|synonymous]] with ''M. multiceps'').<ref name="Hunt">{{cite book | last1=Hunt | first1=David R.|author-link1=David Hunt (botanist) | last2=Taylor | first2=Nigel P. | last3=Charles | first3=G. | title=The New Cactus Lexicon | publisher=Dh Books | issue=v. 2 | year=2006 | isbn=978-0-9538134-6-9 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=up6vtQEACAAJ | access-date=17 January 2025 | pages=171–172}}</ref> ''M. prolifera'' subsp. ''arachnoidea'' was originally described in 1978 as a [[variety (botany)|variety]] following chromosome studies, and is unique in being [[diploid]]. ''M. prolifera'' subsp. ''prolifera'' and ''M. prolifera'' subsp. ''texana'' are [[polyploid]]s, 6x and 4x, respectively.<ref name="Pilbeam"/> Two more subspecies were described. Of these, subsp. ''haitiensis'' is now considered synonymous with subsp. ''prolifera''.<ref name="Hunt"/><ref name="JohnPilbeam"/> The other has been found to represent a distinct species, ''[[Mammillaria zublerae|M. zublerae]]'', and to be more closely related to ''[[Mammillaria vetula|M. vetula]]''.<ref name="Hunt"/>

==Description==
[[File:Mammillaria prolifera145108652.jpg|thumb|This cactus frequently bears flowers and fruit at the same time.]]
''Mammillaria prolifera'' is a [[succulent]] [[subshrub]].<ref name="POWO">{{cite web | title=Mammillaria prolifera (Mill.) Haw. | website=Plants of the World Online | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:134999-1 | access-date=19 January 2025}}</ref> It was originally described by Miller as a "roundish prolific Cactus, with oval tubercles closely joined, having long white beards" and "tufts of white down on the knobs, and also between them at every joint, which makes the whole plant appear as if it was covered with fine cotton". This description refers to plants brought to [[London]] by [[William Houstoun (botanist)|William Houston]], likely from Cuba. It is now recognized that this is a highly [[variable species]].<ref name="JohnPilbeam"/> It usually grows in dense clusters, with each stem being round to slightly elongated, reaching about 9{{nbsp}}cm tall and 4.5{{nbsp}}cm wide. The surface is covered in small, cylindrical bumps ([[tubercle]]s) about 1{{nbsp}}cm long, and their bases are either bare or have fine white hairs that can be as long or longer than the bumps themselves.<ref name="Hunt"/> The roots are [[fibrous root system|fibrous]].<ref name="FNA"/> The fruit is edible,<ref name="Prisa">{{cite journal | last1=Prisa | first1=Domenico | last2=Spagnuolo | first2=Damiano | title=Evaluation of the Bio-Stimulating Activity of Lake Algae Extracts on Edible Cacti Mammillaria prolifera and Mammillaria glassii | journal=Plants | publisher=MDPI AG | volume=11 | issue=24 | date=19 December 2022 | issn=2223-7747 | doi=10.3390/plants11243586 | doi-access=free | page=3586| pmid=36559698 | pmc=9782507 | bibcode=2022Plnts..11.3586P }}</ref> cylindric, measuring 8–20{{nbsp}}mm long and 4–5{{nbsp}}mm wide, juicy only in the outer walls, and the dried flower remains attached.<ref name="FNA"/> The subspecies differ primarily in the shape and number of [[thorns, spines, and prickles|spines]].<ref name="Hunt"/> 
[[File:Mammillaria prolifera20100315.jpg|thumb|left|The seed is small and its color–unlike those of the flowers, fruit, and spines–invariable.]]
''Mammillaria prolifera'' subsp. ''prolifera'' may form clusters or remain simple.<ref name="Hunt"/> It has a rounded to short, cylindrical shape, growing up to 6–7{{nbsp}}cm wide. The spaces between its bumps ([[axils]]) are filled with short wool and white bristles. It has many radial spines—around 60 or more—that are white, bristle-like to fine and hair-like, and can be straight or twisted, ranging from 6–15{{nbsp}}mm long. Its central spines number between 6 and 11, are needle-like, and one is thicker and longer than the rest. These spines are slightly fuzzy, glassy white to pale [[straw-yellow]] at the base, and have darker tips, measuring 4–7{{nbsp}}mm long.<ref name="Hunt"/><ref name="Pilbeam"/> Its flowers are cream yellow with a reddish brown midstripe, approximately 15{{nbsp}}mm long and just as wide. The fruit is orange-red and may last until the plant blooms again the next year. The seed is black.<ref name="Pilbeam"/>

''Mammillaria prolifera'' subsp. ''arachnoidea'' is set apart from the other subspecies primarily by the smaller size of its stems and an overall softer appearance.<ref name="JohnPilbeam"/> It has 4–5 extremely thin central spines.<ref name="Hunt"/> They are almost indistinguishable from the radial spines,<ref name="Pilbeam"/> which in turn resemble a [[cobweb]].<ref name="JohnPilbeam"/><ref name="Hunt"/> Its flowers are shaped like a narrow funnel.<ref name="Hunt"/>
[[File:Mammillaria prolifera in Tamaulipas.jpg|thumb|The species is inconspicuous in its natural habitat.]]
''Mammillaria prolifera'' subsp. ''texana'' is distinguished by its greyish color. It is densely clustering all along the stem. The stems are 5–7{{nbsp}}cm in diameter and form low, almost flat clumps. The bristles in the axils are white. It has over 50 thin, needle-like radial spines per areola; these are 5–9 mm{{nbsp}}long and white. The areola usually has 8–12 needle-like central spines, which are 4–7{{nbsp}}mm long, white and somewhat sturdier than the radial spines. Their tips are brown. All spines are straight and smooth. The flowers, about 20{{nbsp}}mm long and 15{{nbsp}}mm wide, have white edges and a brownish pink midstripe.<ref name="Pilbeam"/> They appear throughout spring,<ref name="FNA"/> and are followed by red fruit and black seed.<ref name="Pilbeam"/> This subspecies is especially [[free-flowering|freely]] fruiting.<ref name="Hunt"/> A yellow-spined form exists, with pale yellow radial spines, honey yellow central spines, and creamy yellow to pale yellow flowers.<ref name="Pilbeam"/> This form has not been named.<ref name="JohnPilbeam"/>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Mammillaria prolifera'' is native to [[Texas]], northeastern [[states of Mexico]], [[Cuba]], and [[Hispaniola]]. It grows primarily in the tropical biome that undergoes seasonal droughts.<ref name="POWO"/> ''Mammillaria prolifera'' subsp. ''prolifera'' is found in [[Cuba]], [[Dominican Republic]], and [[Haiti]],<ref name="Hunt" /> typically at elevations between 30{{nbsp}}m and 50{{nbsp}}m [[above sea level]].<ref name="Pilbeam" /> Britton and Rose noted its presence at [[Guantanamo Bay Naval Base]]. They described it as growing in low, dry thickets, where it is "quite inconspicuous but abundant".<ref name="Britton">{{cite book | last1=Britton | first1=Nathaniel L. | last2=Rose | first2=Joseph N. |author-link1=Nathaniel Lord Britton|author2-link=Joseph Nelson Rose| title=The Cactaceae: Descriptions and Illustrations of Plants of the Cactus Family | publisher=Carnegie Institution of Washington | volume=4 | year=1923 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yS0mAQAAMAAJ | access-date=18 January 2025 | page=124}}</ref> Specific locations include [[Port-au-Prince]] and [[Ganthier]] in Haiti and [[Guayubin]] in the Dominican Republic.<ref name="Pilbeam" /> ''Mammillaria prolifera'' subsp. ''arachnoidea'' has been collected in the Mexican states of [[Hidalgo (state)|Hidalgo]] (in the canyon of the [[Moctezuma River]], east of [[Jacala]]) and [[Tamaulipas]] (8{{nbsp}}km west of [[Antiguo Morelos]], on rocks next to [[Mexican Federal Highway 8|Federal Highway 8]]) at 300{{nbsp}}m above sea level.<ref name="Hunt" /><ref name="Pilbeam" />[[File:Mammillaria prolifera multiceps.jpg|thumb|''M. prolifera'' subsp. ''texana'', seen here in a rock crevice, grows in widely different habitats.]]

The distribution of ''Mammillaria prolifera'' subsp. ''texana'' extends from the [[US state]] of [[Texas]] to the Mexican states of [[Coahuila]], [[Nuevo León]], [[Querétaro]], [[San Luis Potosí]], and Tamaulipas at 400–2250{{nbsp}}m above sea level.<ref name="FNA"/><ref name="Pilbeam"/> In Texas it is found at 0–600{{nbsp}}m in the [[Tamaulipan thorn scrub]], oak-juniper woodlands, gravel, limestone crevices, or litter beneath vegetation, cliffs, hills, valleys, and plains.<ref name="FNA">{{cite book | title=Flora of North America: North of Mexico | publisher=Oxford University Press | volume= 4 | year=1993 | isbn=978-0-19-517389-5 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GCklAQAAMAAJ | access-date=19 January 2025 | page=254}}</ref> It grows all along the [[Rio Grande]] and along the [[Gulf Coast of Texas]] to the vicinity of [[Rockport, Texas|Rockport]], never straying more than a few miles from the coast. Here it thrives in rich, deep lowland soils near thickets or among the clumps of coastal grasses on the flat plains near the Gulf. At [[Eagle Pass, Texas|Eagle Pass]] it diverges from the river, and it is found on the rocky hilltops of the [[Edwards Escarpment]], wedged into [[limestone]] crevices, often in very little soil and shaded by the rocks. It reaches north almost to [[Bandera, Texas|Bandera]] and [[Rocksprings]], where winters become too cold for it to survive.<ref name="Weniger">{{cite book | last=Weniger | first=Del | title=Cacti of the Southwest | publisher=University of Texas Press | year=1970 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=C85GswEACAAJ | access-date=19 January 2025 | pages=147–149}}</ref> The yellow-spined form may be found both alone and together with the brown-spined form,<ref name="Weniger"/> and the two do not appear to interbreed.<ref name="Pilbeam"/> The ecologist Den Weniger, who observed the two forms in the wild, suggests that they might be [[phenotype]]s of the same variable population.<ref name="Weniger"/>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Mammillarias in pots.jpg|thumb|''M. prolifera'' and ''M. vetula'' are credited with introducing many cacti fanciers to the genus.]]
''Mammillaria prolifera'' is one of the best known, easiest to grow, and most commonly cultivated ''Mammillaria'' species. The cacti nurseryman and journalist John Pilbeam notes that because of this it is "almost looked down upon by the connoisseurs".<ref name="JohnPilbeam">{{cite journal | last=Pilbeam | first=John| title=Mammillaria prolifera from Cuba | journal=British Cactus & Succulent Journal | publisher=British Cactus and Succulent Society | volume=18 | issue=3 | year=2000 | issn=0264-3405 | jstor=42793680 | pages=159–161 }}</ref> It is appreciated for its attractively dense tufts of spines and its ability to produce flowers and fruit simultaneously and more abundantly than any other ''Mammillaria'' species.<ref name="Pilbeam">{{cite book | last=Pilbeam | first=John | title=Mammillaria | publisher=Cirio Publishing Services | series=Cactus file handbook | year=1999 | isbn=978-0-9528302-8-3 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-hBFAAAAYAAJ | access-date=17 January 2025 | pages=241–243}}</ref> Like [[Mammillaria vetula subsp. gracilis|''M. vetula'' subsp. ''gracilis'']],  ''M. prolifera'' is easy to propagate and distribute; Pilbeam estimates that most cacti fanciers become interested in the genus after growing these two species. The most commonly cultivated subspecies is ''M. mammillaria'' subsp. ''texana''. According to Pilbeam, ''M. mammillaria'' subsp. ''arachnoidea'' is more challenging to grow than the other subspecies.<ref name="JohnPilbeam" />
